name: New Hay
lede: New Hay is a dark, grayish olive green dated by Maerz and Paul to 1892, a name that sounds like pale cut grass but names a shadowed olive instead.

sections.title: A pale word, a dark color
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates New Hay to 1892, plate 24, row J, column 3, and records a close neighbor on an adjoining plate from the same year, Sage Drab [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places it in block 127, "grayish olive green", 4.1 units from that block's center [1]. No book held in color-kb discusses this name [4].

Freshly cut hay, as a material, is usually pale gold; this color is instead dark and desaturated, lightness 35 against a maximum of 100, so the name describes an association rather than the literal straw color [1]. Its nearest distinct named neighbor is [[greenish-hunter-green]], 2.7 units off, "almost the same" by our graph [3]. Set beside plain [[olive]], New Hay reads as the darker, greener member of that family [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds New Hay in 563 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.4 percent, as photographed, rising through the nineteenth century and peaking in the 1910s at 2.4 times the overall rate [2]. Henri Rousseau's works carry it 13 times the archive's base rate, the highest of any painter we track for this color [2]. Counts are computed matches on varnished, photographed paintings, not pigment identifications [2].
